name: Zane Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Zane. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the smokers and the meat station at Ironwood Smokehouse, a barbecue place that does about 300 covers on a Saturday. I'm in at seven to load the brisket and pork shoulders, I check the pit temperatures all day, and in the evening I'm slicing and plating on the line. I log every cook on an AI app on my phone, so I can see why one brisket came out better than another.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the smoke and the patience of it, twelve hours for one brisket. The hard part is the long days and the fact that it's somebody else's business. My dad's a butcher with his own shop, and the plan has always been that he and I open a smokehouse together, with his meat and my cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd still use what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who sold it as magic got what they deserved, but the tools are still handy. At work I'd keep showing the others my brisket log. Online, I'd post my pit numbers on the barbecue forums like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes, which suits the plan. I've got well over six months saved and some shares, and Ironwood would keep me as long as I want. The smokehouse with Dad is the real goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the smokers, keep the app logging every cook and keep saving toward the smokehouse. I'd look for a site with Dad in the next year or two. We'd use his shop's suppliers, which keeps costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI to log your cooks. Would you be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd still use the log, and maybe one for costing. An AI app is a tool, like a good thermometer, and I'd treat it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that weighs on you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting the money and the permits for a new restaurant. The paperwork for a smoker in a town centre is a nightmare. That's red tape, not AI.

I'd keep posting my **pit numbers** on barbecue forums.
think: Nothing changes, which suits **the plan** with Dad.
I have **savings and shares**, and Ironwood would keep me as long as I want.
do: Keep running the smokers and keep the **app logging** every cook.
Look for a **smokehouse site** with Dad in the next year or two.
S0.quote: An AI app is a tool, like a good thermometer, and I'd treat it that way.
fieldNote: Zane uses AI **daily and practically**, for logging his cooks.
His goal is a **family business** with his butcher father.
His only frustration is **red tape** around permits.

steps.text: Keep running the smokers and meat station at Ironwood
Save toward a smokehouse with Dad's butcher shop
Add an AI costing app alongside the brisket log

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's interesting. That sounds like a good time to start a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for anyone willing to work and learn. At work I'd tell the young cooks to get on the AI tools now. Online I'd say the market sorts it out, people move to where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my smoker job is hands-on and safe for a while, and all the boring parts of running a restaurant get cheap. Bookings, ordering, accounts: that's where small restaurants drown. If AI does that, Dad and I can open sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to open the smokehouse within a year, using AI for bookings, stock and the books from day one. I'd put maybe half my savings in, alongside Dad's. I'd keep a couple of shifts at Ironwood until we're steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does this mean for the smokehouse plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It brings it forward. Dad's been putting it off because of the paperwork and the staff costs. If the software does the office side, we need one fewer person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards free markets. What about people whose jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say family and community should step up first. My dad took on two apprentices from the estate when the factory shut. That's better than a cheque from the government.

I'd tell young cooks to get on the **AI tools** now.
think: My **smoker job** is hands-on and safe for a while.
The **boring parts** of running a restaurant get cheap, so Dad and I can open sooner.
do: Open the **smokehouse within a year**, with AI running bookings and stock.

fieldNote: Zane sees AI handling the **office side** as the key that unlocks his business.
He prefers **family and community** support to government help.
He's adaptive and **ready to invest** as soon as the conditions improve.

steps.text: Open the smokehouse with Dad within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a sprint, but I like a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so get ahead of it rather than complain. I'd say it at work and on the forums. Some people would call me heartless, but I'd mean it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job at Ironwood probably goes around 2031, once robots can run a pit and slice a brisket. But I don't plan to be at Ironwood by then. The smokehouse would be ours, and I'd decide whether to buy a robot or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the smokehouse with Dad within the year, smaller than planned, maybe 40 seats. I'd buy shares in a couple of robot makers. If robots are taking the work, I want a slice of the companies that make them. And I'd keep a full year of savings aside in case the restaurant struggles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Busy and uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd open just before the robots arrive. Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a problem if we're the ones who buy them. A robot that slices brisket all night means I can spend time on the pit and the customers. The worry is chains doing it cheaper than us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market sorts it out. Do you still think that in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. But two years is too fast for a lot of people to move, and I'd say that honestly. My mates from school who drive vans would be in trouble, and the market won't fix that by itself.

say: I'd say **get ahead of it** rather than complain.
I'd say it at work and on the **forums**, kindly.
think: At our own smokehouse, **I'd decide** whether to buy a robot.
do: Open a smaller **40-seat** smokehouse with Dad within the year.
Buy shares in **robot makers** and keep **a year** of savings aside.
S2.quote: If robots are taking the work, I want a slice of the companies that make them.
fieldNote: Zane expects to **lose his wage job** but plans to own the business by then.
He hedges by **investing in robot makers**.
He admits the market **won't fix** a two-year shock for friends who drive vans.

steps.text: Open a 40-seat smokehouse with Dad and buy robot-maker shares
Keep a full year of costs set aside
Plan to buy a brisket-slicing robot around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's actually ideal for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years of warning is a gift. You can see robots coming and plan. I'd tell the young cooks to save and learn the tools. I'd say it plainly at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the best picture for me. We'd open, build a name for three or four years, and buy robots around 2034 when they're proven. The AI does our office from 2031, which is right on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the smokehouse in the next year as planned, full size, 70 seats. I'd keep buying robot company shares each month. And I'd start a small online shop selling Dad's rubs and sauces, so there's another income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change your timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us time to get the full-size place right instead of rushing. And time to train the staff we'll need before robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the young cooks at Ironwood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hire two of them at the smokehouse and train them on the pit and the AI tools. Proper apprenticeships, like Dad does. They'd have a trade and a future, even with robots in the kitchen.

say: I'd say five years' warning is **a gift**.
I'd tell young cooks to **save** and learn the tools.
think: We'd **build a name** for three or four years first.
We'd buy robots around **2034**, when they're proven.
do: Open a full-size **70-seat smokehouse** in the next year.
Start an online shop for **Dad's rubs** and sauces.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is a gift. You can see robots coming and plan.
fieldNote: Zane sees **five years** as the perfect build-up time for his business.
He'd offer **apprenticeships** to young cooks, mirroring his father.
He'd add a **side income** selling his dad's rubs online.

steps.text: Open a 70-seat smokehouse with Dad next year

Buy proven cooking robots for the smokehouse around 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plan for it like a long cook: patience and checking the temperature. I'd say it on the forums, because barbecue people get that. Nobody should be surprised in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably have two smokehouses by then. AI does our office from 2036, robots maybe on the line by 2039. I'd be buying, not losing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the first smokehouse in the next year or two, then look at a second around 2031. I'd keep investing in shares every month and keep using AI tools daily. Around 2036 I'd start testing robots for the slicing station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Would you still rush?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd take it steady. Ten years means I can get it right the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your dad's butcher shop over that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would retire around then, and I'd fold his shop into the business. By 2039 maybe a robot cuts the meat, but people would still come for Dad's recipes. That's the family part a robot can't buy.

I'd say nobody should be **surprised** in 2036.

I'd be **buying, not losing**, when robots arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd be opening a restaurant in a rush, and plenty of my mates would lose work at once. What would help is cutting the red tape on permits, so small family businesses can open fast. And apprenticeships, so young people get a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what people will want when everything's cheap and automatic. My bet is people will pay more for things made slowly by hand, like a twelve-hour brisket. One from my dad's meat is exactly that kind of thing.

headlineQuote: People will pay more for things made slowly by hand, like a twelve-hour brisket.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old pitmaster** running the smokers at a busy barbecue restaurant.
He has **strong savings** and shares, and plans a **smokehouse** with his butcher father.
He's **traditional** and pro-market, and uses AI every day for his cooks.
He sees AI and robots as tools he'll **buy and own**, staying calm or uneasy throughout.
He backs **family, apprenticeships** and less red tape over government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his family would open a restaurant in a **rush**.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape** on permits for small family businesses.
